## Sorting

Sorting an encrypted vector can provide useful information, including its minimum, maximum, median, and quartiles. But ordinary sorting algorithms often branch on comparison results or use encrypted values as memory indices, operations that are unavailable in FHE. We instead must attempt to sort using only arithmetic operations on encrypted values.

We will compare methods by their total comparisons, sequential comparison layers, and arithmetic depth. The chapters develop these ideas in order: PairSort and bubble sort, parallel schedules, rank-based sorting, then maximum extraction. The discrete-model section gives a comparison construction for bounded integer inputs; here the focus is how sorting methods use comparisons.


### Comparison Based Sorting

The first intuitive method is to utilize sorts that compare and order pairs of values on a schedule irrelevant of the input of the data. Sorts such as merge and quicksort are not suitable for FHE because their branching depends on the results of the comparison. In FHE, comparisons can be expressed as an arithmetic operation using a polynomial approximation of the sign function.

We call this arithmetic operation on a pair of values PairSort, defined in the [bubble sort chapter](bubble.qmd#sec-pairsort). It can be used to emulate sorts prevalent in sorting networks, which allow for a fixed schedule of comparisons regardless of the results. 

### Rank and place

A different strategy exists that avoids moving values through successive swaps. It compares each pair, counts how many values are smaller than each input, then places each value at its rank. This uses fewer independent comparisons, as all the comparisons are independent and can be computed in parallel. However, this requires for a ciphertext $n$, the ability to compute on a vector of size $n^2$. It can be preferable when the input suits the size constraint, as it can allow for less comparison depth than swap based methods. One can return all the ranks of the inputs as its own result, but taking this encrypted rank and using it to place the indexes in their sorted positions is also considered.

### Maximum and minimum

A consequence of sorting is that the maximum and minimum values are available at the end of the sort. However, we can also compute the maximum and minimum in $O(\log(n))$ time using a tournament style comparison, which is more efficient than sorting.
